Social structure. Social structure refers to the enduring patterns of roles, relationships, and institutions that organize a society and give it coherence and stability. Anthropologists have shown that societies are not just collections of individuals making independent choices, but rather systems held together by interlocking statuses, kinship rules, rituals, and power hierarchies. A.R. Radcliffe-Brown pioneered this understanding, emphasizing that to understand why people behave as they do, you must grasp not just individual psychology but the slots people occupy in a larger web of social organization.

Social structure encompasses kinship systems that determine who can marry whom and inheritance rules, economic roles like producer, merchant, and elder, political hierarchies from chief to council to commoner, and ritual specialists like priests and healers. These elements work together as an integrated system. Radcliffe-Brown pioneered the analysis of social structure as a logical whole, arguing that institutions and practices maintain social integration and must be studied in relation to one another, not in isolation. Pull one thread and the whole fabric changes. Rites of passage both reflect and reinforce social structure by marking transitions between statuses. A boy becomes a warrior, a woman becomes a mother, a living person becomes an ancestor. These ceremonies are not peripheral but central to how society perpetuates itself.

Roles within social structure are not freely chosen. They carry prescribed behaviors, rights, and obligations tied to one's position. A chief is constrained to act chiefly, a guest to act as a guest. These constraints are not written down but deeply internalized. Status can be ascribed, given at birth through caste, gender, or family position, or achieved through accomplishment like becoming a skilled warrior or wealthy merchant. The distinction matters because it shapes what futures seem possible. Social structures vary dramatically across societies. Some are egalitarian with minimal hierarchy, others are rigidly stratified into castes or classes. Some emphasize kinship as the primary organizing principle, others property or age.

Modern societies also have social structure expressed through occupational hierarchies, class stratification, and racial stratification, though it is often less visible because it is less sacralized by ritual and is contested, resisted, and constantly negotiated. Understanding social structure is foundational to anthropology because what looks like individual choice is often constrained by invisible webs of expectation, obligation, and role.
